title: Statistical inference and resource allocation in expert data production
markdown:
## 1 The observation mechanism creates its own failure modes In production RLHF pipelines, the routing policy used to inspect submissions alters the statistical properties of the observed sample. Let $`X`$ denote observable task features (encoding domain vertical, prompt complexity, and contributor history) and $`Y \in \{0, 1\}`$ indicate an error in the original submission under fixed acceptance criteria. The true conditional error probability is $`q(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)`$. Let $`S = 1`$ indicate selection for an independent reference audit. Conditional on $`X`$, selection is randomized with probability $`\pi(x) > 0`$, independently of the reference label that has yet to be observed. When operational dashboards use the error fraction among verified submissions to assess the full population, they actually target: $$ E[Y \mid S = 1] = \frac{E[\pi(X)q(X)]}{E[\pi(X)]} $$ $$ E[Y \mid S = 1] - E[Y] = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\pi(X), q(X))}{E[\pi(X)]} $$ When review priorities successfully target high-risk tasks, the covariance between audit probability $`\pi(X)`$ and true defect probability $`q(X)`$ is strictly positive. A higher error detection rate in the reviewed sample cannot then be read directly as a deterioration in overall production quality; it often reflects sharper risk targeting. This identity describes the distribution of a selected item. In a finite batch, the ratio of observed errors to selected items also has a random denominator, so the two quantities should not be conflated. Expert rankings are affected by the exact same mechanism. Let $`a_{jh}`$ be the probability that expert $`j`$ is correct on task stratum $`h`$, and let $`p_{jht}`$ describe the mix of tasks assigned to that expert in period $`t`$. Even with unchanged underlying ability, observed accuracy shifts whenever task routing changes: $$ A_{jt} = \sum_h p_{jht} a_{jh}, \qquad A_{j,t+1} - A_{jt} = \sum_h (p_{jh,t+1} - p_{jht}) a_{jh} $$ Valid cross-period comparisons therefore require a fixed target task mix $`w_h`$, reporting standardized accuracy: $$ A_j^{\text{std}} = \sum_h w_h a_{jh} $$ with overlapping assignments or shared anchor cases to support estimation within each stratum. In our production routing engine, we model each contributor's stratum-level reliability via a conjugate Beta-Binomial scheme: given prior $`\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_{0h}, \beta_{0h})`$ and $`n_{jht}`$ audited tasks with $`k_{jht}`$ verified successes, the posterior reliability distribution $`\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha_{0h} + k_{jht}, \beta_{0h} + n_{jht} - k_{jht})`$ yields shrinkage-regularized point estimates and credible intervals that account for unequal sample sizes across comparable audits. Pooling different difficulty levels, criteria versions, and selection mechanisms into a single unstratified binomial sample leaves the preceding selection bias unresolved. These distinctions also guide algorithmic method selection. **[Dawid-Skene](https://doi.org/10.2307/2346806)** models represent differences in reviewer confusion matrices across latent ground truth, whereas **[DeCCaF](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.06906v1)** incorporates task conditions, error costs, and reviewer capacity into human-AI deferral and highlights how assigning difficult cases distorts naive evaluations of expert performance. The architecture developed here addresses the critical interface between selective operational deferral and unbiased population quality inference in ongoing post-training production (*[Dawid-Skene](https://doi.org/10.2307/2346806); [DeCCaF](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.06906v1)*). ## 2 Correct predictions with audits to recover the population target Fix a production batch of $`N`$ original submissions, its acceptance criteria, and its latent reference labels $`Y_1, \dots, Y_N`$. The inferential target is the finite-batch error rate $`\mu = N^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^N Y_i`$. Let $`f_i \in [0, 1]`$ be a fixed, inexpensive risk prediction (synthesized from contributor posterior reliability, task complexity features, and automated heuristic checks) and $`\pi_i \in [\pi_{\min}, 1]`$ be the assigned audit probability, with independent draws $`S_i \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)`$. Both predictions and sampling probabilities are locked before the current batch's reference labels are revealed. We deploy a prediction-assisted, inverse-probability-weighted (IPW) residual-corrected estimator: $$ \hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ f_i + \frac{S_i}{\pi_i} (Y_i - f_i) \right] $$ Its design-based validity follows directly. Write the prediction residual as $`e_i = Y_i - f_i`$ and condition on the fixed batch, predictions, and sampling probabilities: $$ \hat{\mu} - \mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \frac{S_i}{\pi_i} - 1 \right) e_i, \qquad E_S[\hat{\mu} - \mu] = 0 $$ Inverse-probability weighting restores the population representation altered by selective verification, while predictions reduce the residual variation that expensive human expert audits must resolve. Crucially for production robustness, **this design-based unbiasedness does not require $`f_i = q(X_i)`$**: inaccurate predictions can reduce statistical efficiency, but they never introduce selection bias under the specified Bernoulli sampling design. While the estimator builds on established active statistical inference principles (*[Active Statistical Inference: mean estimation and sampling design](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.03208v3)*), our production architecture specifies the exact immutable objects being audited, the rubric version lineage, and the telemetry records required for downstream optimization. Specifically, original and revised submissions must be retained as separate database entities. Estimating $`\hat{\mu}_{\text{raw}}`$ on frozen originals and $`\hat{\mu}_{\text{final}}`$ on post-review deliverables cleanly distinguishes *defects generated in initial production* from *defects corrected by review*. Furthermore, whenever post-training criteria evolve, a shared set of anchor cases is adjudicated under both rubric versions; submissions from different periods are then compared under a common reference version, preventing stricter acceptance standards from being mistaken for declining contributor capability. ## 3 Allocate audit effort according to residuals and cost Independent Bernoulli sampling eliminates cross-item covariance terms, yielding the exact design variance: $$ \operatorname{Var}_S(\hat{\mu}) = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1 - \pi_i}{\pi_i} e_i^2 $$ This expression identifies the true mathematical objective of audit allocation: **audit effort should address what the automated risk predictions have not resolved**. For a binary error label with conditional error probability $`q_i`$, the expected squared residual decomposes into two components: $$ m_i := E[(Y_i - f_i)^2 \mid X_i] = q_i(1 - q_i) + (q_i - f_i)^2 $$ The two terms are intrinsic conditional Bernoulli variance $`q_i(1 - q_i)`$ and squared prediction calibration error $`(q_i - f_i)^2`$. This identity establishes a counter-intuitive operational principle: **a high error probability $`q_i`$ does not necessarily imply high inferential value**. If a task category is almost certain to contain an error ($`q_i \approx 1`$) and the predictor correctly recognizes that fact ($`f_i \approx 1`$), then $`m_i \approx 0`$—spending an independent reference audit on that item yields less statistical information about population quality than auditing a moderately risky task whose outcome is genuinely uncertain ($`q_i \approx 0.5`$). The high-risk task still merits operational correction, which is precisely why the *value of measurement* and the *value of remediation* require separate mathematical models. Let $`c_i > 0`$ be the empirical cost of an independent reference audit (calibrated by reconciling platform review logs with Hubstaff active-work telemetry) and $`B`$ be the expected audit-cost budget. First consider the optimal design when the true residual second moments $`m_i > 0`$ are known: $$ \min_{\pi} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{m_i}{\pi_i} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i=1}^N c_i \pi_i \le B, \quad \pi_{\min} \le \pi_i \le 1 $$ The omitted constant $`-\sum_i m_i`$ in the numerator of the variance does not depend on the allocation $`\pi`$. For probabilities strictly between their lower and upper bounds, the Lagrangian first-order condition yields the clipped square-root allocation law: $$ -\frac{m_i}{\pi_i^2} + \lambda c_i = 0 \implies \pi_i^* = \operatorname{clip}_{[\pi_{\min}, 1]} \left( \sqrt{\frac{m_i}{\lambda c_i}} \right) $$ for budgets below the cost of a full audit, $`\lambda > 0`$ is chosen to satisfy the budget constraint (the multiplier need not be unique when clipping is active), and feasibility requires $`B \ge \pi_{\min} \sum_i c_i`$. If the budget covers a full audit, every item is audited ($`\pi_i^* = 1`$). The square-root law increases sampling intensity for larger expected residuals while penalizing expensive audits, and the positive probability floor $`\pi_{\min}`$ preserves observation coverage and bounded IPW weights across the entire task space. Production implementation substitutes regularized stratum estimates $`\hat{m}_i > 0`$ obtained from earlier independent audits or a pilot calibration batch. True $`m_i`$ defines the optimality analysis; estimated values $`\hat{m}_i`$ determine the operational allocation. By estimating residuals at the level of `(task stratum × criteria version × cost stratum)`, the pipeline avoids fitting unstable parameters to individual submissions. (Note that $`B`$ constrains *expected* audit cost per batch. Workflows requiring an exact integer count must use a feasible fixed-size sampling design: its first-order inclusion probabilities sum to that integer, and its variance depends on joint inclusion probabilities. These probabilities need not equal the Bernoulli optimum $`\pi_i^*`$.) ## 4 Derive the gain and identify when it disappears We now derive the exact analytical efficiency gain of cost-aware residual allocation over uniform sampling using the same predictor, and characterize when active allocation fails. Let $`C = \sum_{i=1}^N c_i`$, so that the budget-equivalent uniform sampling probability is $`p = B / C`$. When true residual second moments $`m_i`$ are available and no optimal probability reaches a clipping boundary, averaging design variance over the conditional label distribution gives: $$ V_{\text{uniform}} = \frac{1}{N^2} \left[ \frac{C \sum_i m_i}{B} - \sum_i m_i \right] $$ $$ V_{\text{optimal}} = \frac{1}{N^2} \left[ \frac{\left(\sum_i \sqrt{m_i c_i}\right)^2}{B} - \sum_i m_i \right] $$ (If a common sampling probability is used within each fixed task stratum, substituting that stratum's finite-batch mean squared residual for $`m_i`$ makes these expressions exact finite-batch identities.) By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality: $$ V_{\text{uniform}} - V_{\text{optimal}} = \frac{C \sum_i m_i - \left(\sum_i \sqrt{m_i c_i}\right)^2}{N^2 B} \ge 0 $$ Equality holds **if and only if $`m_i / c_i`$ is constant across all items**. Efficiency gains therefore depend strictly on identifiable heterogeneity in residual second moment per unit audit cost; with homogeneous residuals and costs, optimal allocation reduces to uniform sampling. When clipping is active at $`\pi_{\min}`$ or $`1`$, constrained optimization is still no worse than feasible uniform policies, with the exact gain evaluated directly at the clipped primal objective. Crucially, the same analysis exposes the exact variance penalty of model misspecification. If the allocation uses inaccurate residual estimates $`\hat{m}_i`$ and neither allocation is clipped, the excess variance relative to the true optimum is: $$ V(\hat{\pi}) - V(\pi^*) = \frac{1}{N^2 B} \left[ \left( \sum_i \sqrt{\hat{m}_i c_i} \right) \left( \sum_i \frac{m_i \sqrt{c_i}}{\sqrt{\hat{m}_i}} \right) - \left( \sum_i \sqrt{m_i c_i} \right)^2 \right] \ge 0 $$ Severely underestimating $`\hat{m}_i`$ in any region of the task space inflates the penalty through the $`\sqrt{\hat{m}_i}`$ denominator. Enforcing a positive sampling floor $`\pi_{\min}`$ caps this worst-case blowup, while mixing active and uniform probabilities via the budget-preserving defensive convex combination: $$ \pi_i(\rho) = (1 - \rho)\hat{\pi}_i + \rho p $$ allows the shrinkage weight $`\rho \in [0, 1]`$ to be tuned across independent calibration batches (*[Robust Sampling for Active Statistical Inference](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.08991v1)*). ## 5 Allocate review by expected loss reduction Whereas statistical auditing seeks to *measure* population quality with minimum variance, operational review seeks to *remove defects* from the current batch before training handoff. For task $`i`$ under handling action $`a`$ (e.g., accept directly, route to peer review, escalate to expert adjudication, or request contributor revision), let $`r_{ia}`$ be the expected error loss remaining *after* the action, $`d_{ia}`$ its operational cost, and $`t_{iaj}`$ the time required from specialist $`j`$ (measured via platform and Hubstaff telemetry). Binary assignment decisions $`z_{ia} \in \{0, 1\}`$ solve: $$ \min_{z} F(z) = \sum_{i,a} z_{ia}(r_{ia} + \eta d_{ia}) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_a z_{ia} = 1, \quad \sum_{i,a} z_{ia} t_{iaj} \le H_j \quad \forall j $$ where $`H_j`$ is available specialist time and $`\eta \ge 0`$ converts resource cost to the scale of error loss (*[DeCCaF: capacity constraints and global assignment](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.06906v1)*). When review costs are equal and each reviewed task consumes one slot, **the optimal priority ranking is by marginal remediation gain $`\Delta_i = r_{i0} - r_{i1}`$, not by initial risk $`r_{i0}`$**. Missing external evidence may make a high-risk task difficult to repair through one additional review ($`\Delta_i`$ small), whereas a self-contained calculation error in a moderate-risk task can be completely eliminated ($`\Delta_k`$ large). Moving a single review slot from task $`i`$ to task $`k`$ changes total expected loss by: $$ \Delta F = (r_{i0} + r_{k1}) - (r_{i1} + r_{k0}) = \Delta_i - \Delta_k $$ Whenever $`\Delta_k > \Delta_i`$, the exchange strictly reduces delivered defect loss, regardless of the tasks' initial risk ordering. We can also state the exact calibration precision required of the action-risk estimators. Suppose $`|\hat{r}_{ia} - r_{ia}| \le \delta`$ for every feasible action, costs and capacities are known, and $`\hat{z}`$ minimizes the predicted objective $`\hat{F}(z)`$. Relative to the true optimal feasible assignment $`z^*`$: $$ F(\hat{z}) \le \hat{F}(\hat{z}) + N\delta \le \hat{F}(z^*) + N\delta \le F(z^*) + 2N\delta $$ This bound identifies *post-action residual loss* $`r_{ia}`$ as the critical empirical calibration target, motivating randomized pilot trials across permitted review actions. Finally, both budgets—remediation and statistical measurement—combine into a single batch-level **Mixed-Integer Convex Program (MICP)**. Let $`\tau^2`$ be the target variance ceiling for the quality estimate, $`B_{\text{total}}`$ the combined cost budget, and $`V_{\hat{m}}(\pi) = N^{-2}\sum_i (1 - \pi_i)\hat{m}_i / \pi_i`$ the planning variance under the calibrated residual model: $$ \min_{z, \pi} \sum_{i,a} z_{ia}\hat{r}_{ia} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{i,a} z_{ia} d_{ia} + \sum_i c_i \pi_i \le B_{\text{total}}, \quad V_{\hat{m}}(\pi) \le \tau^2 $$ $$ \sum_a z_{ia} = 1, \quad z_{ia} \in \{0, 1\}, \quad \sum_{i,a} z_{ia} t_{iaj} \le H_j^{\text{review}} \ \forall j, \quad \pi_{\min} \le \pi_i \le 1 $$ Here $`H_j^{\text{review}}`$ is hard capacity allocated to remediation actions while reference audits are scheduled independently on frozen original submissions. The precision ceiling is model-based: independent audits must check residual calibration, and expected audit cost does not impose a hard limit on realized audit hours. Infeasibility exposes a conflict between the planning precision target, feasible review assignments, and available engineering budget. ## 6 Reproducible experiments at equal cost The following self-contained synthetic experiments test the mathematical mechanisms derived above (they validate algorithmic behavior on specified public parameters rather than reporting proprietary client telemetry). A fixed batch contains $`N = 10,000`$ submissions partitioned into three strata of $`6,000`$, $`3,000`$, and $`1,000`$ items, containing $`60`$, $`300`$, and $`350`$ errors respectively (true batch defect rate $`\mu = 7.10\%`$). Unit audit costs are $`1`$, $`1.5`$, and $`3`$ units across the three strata. Every policy operates under an expected audit budget of $`B = 2,000`$ units and a minimum sampling floor of $`\pi_{\min} = 3\%`$. Risk predictions for the three strata are $`2\%`$, $`8\%`$, and $`30\%`$ (batch average $`6.60\%`$, differing from the true defect rate by $`0.50`$ percentage points). Cost-aware allocation uses the true within-stratum mean squared residuals (ideal calibration), while the misspecified policy reverses the residual ordering across strata. Holding predictions, budget, and submissions fixed, $`200,000`$ independent Monte Carlo repetitions verify the analytical variance formulas:

Under ideal residual calibration, the standard deviation of the population quality estimate falls by **9.33%** (a **17.79% variance reduction**). Notice that for the naive high-risk-first policy, the uncorrected raw error detection rate averages **19.60%** (wildly distorting true quality), whereas our IPW residual-corrected estimator recovers **7.1015%** while exposing that naive risk-prioritization actually *inflates* estimation variance by **33.77%** due to over-sampling the expensive third stratum. Across all five policies, Monte Carlo variances match analytical formulas to within $`0.5\%`$. A separate, exact allocation experiment isolates remediation gains. Two task groups contain $`100`$ items each, with initial error risks of $`0.40`$ and $`0.15`$. Additional review reduces those risks to $`0.30`$ ($`\Delta_1 = 0.10`$) and $`0.01`$ ($`\Delta_2 = 0.14`$), respectively. Review costs are equal and capacity is $`100`$ items. Ranking by initial risk leaves $`100(0.30) + 100(0.15) = 45`$ expected errors; ranking by expected loss reduction ($`\Delta_i`$) leaves $`100(0.40) + 100(0.01) = 41`$ expected errors—cutting expected defect loss by **8.89%** at the exact same review volume. ## 7 Establish whether the design improves production Production deployment tests statistical quality inference and operational defect control separately, recognizing that *detecting more errors in a targeted queue is never, by itself, evidence of better delivered quality*: 1. **Inferential Validation on Frozen Adjudicated Batches**: Compare uniform sampling, legacy high-risk routing, cost-aware residual allocation, and defensive mixtures against complete independent adjudication—evaluating bias, MSE, and interval coverage across individual task strata and rubric versions. 2. **Capacity-Matched Remediation Trials**: Compare legacy tiered rules against marginal-gain ($`\Delta_i`$) action allocation at equal total specialist hours, measuring severe defects surviving into final post-training corpora and total fully-loaded cost per accepted submission. The contributor reliability records, tiered review workflows, and random reference audits I established from September 2023 provided the operational foundation for this architecture. The mathematical analysis above states the sampling, calibration, and capacity assumptions under which quality estimation is unbiased and audit allocation is optimal when residual second moments are correctly specified; the synthetic benchmarks test those mechanisms under their stated conditions.
